evidence_occurrences.evidence_text: paired it with "good" quality AG runs with a 5 minute time limit.
evidence_occurrences.statement: The polymer author used five-minute AutoGluon runs for data tuning and longer best-quality runs for final models.

evidence_occurrences.evidence_text: **AutoGluon vs. "traditional methods":** AutoGluon's "best" quality preset with a 2 hour limit for each property was able to beat an ensemble of XGBoost, LightGBM, and TabM models that I tuned with Optuna and ~20x that amount of compute (not counting data preprocessing tuning, which was in the ballpark of ~1 day per downstream prediction library I paired it with, or all the other models I tried before settling on XGB + LGBM + TabM for the relatively manual ensemble). Its wMAE score was ~2% better than the relatively manual ensemble, good enough that it was not useful to make an ensemble of AutoGluon + my more manually constructed ensemble. The "best" quality AutoGluon runs are very slow, so to let the data tuning run in a reasonable timeframe with a decent trial count I paired it with "good" quality AG runs with a 5 minute time limit. This was my first time using AutoGluon, and I found it very impressive. The level of effort invested in the manual ensemble was maybe only a third of what I used to win the UM MCTS competition, so it is plausible I could beat it if I really pulled out all the stops and wasn't distracted by non-tabular experiments, but I was absolutely gob-smacked by AutoGluon's efficiency. The "extreme" quality present introduced in AG 1.4.0 is supposedly even more accurate and efficient, but I did not observe any benefits when I tried switching over to it (possibly because the feature counts were too high for it to use all of its models - I saw some errors about that), so the tabular predictor in my final ensemble was created with the "best" quality preset.
